html:
The layered network of periodic markets that tied rural China together in Ming and Qing times. Villages traded at a small standard market town; those towns fed larger intermediate markets; those fed central market cities, and so on up to the great regional cities.

Each standard market served a cluster of perhaps a dozen to twenty villages, close enough that a farmer could walk there and back in a day. Markets met on fixed days in a cycle, often every few days, and neighbouring towns staggered their days so that peddlers and traders could move from one to the next. Farmers sold grain, vegetables and cloth and bought salt, tools and things from further away. The market town was also where people met matchmakers, joined temple festivals and heard news.

The anthropologist G. William Skinner mapped this system in the 1960s, using ideas from central place theory, which says that settlements arrange themselves in ladders of size and service.

The historian Fernand Braudel used the Chinese case to show that markets everywhere tend to stack into such ladders. The Chinese network was dense and busy, with long-distance trade flowing up and down the Grand Canal and the Yangtze, yet it never produced the large merchant capitalism of the European cities he studied. That contrast is one of his main questions.
